know_how.title: Restaurants
know_how.text: Bread, olives, cheese or butter put on the table (the couvert) are charged if you eat them. Send them back if you don't want them. Tipping is not required; 5 to 10% for good service is a kind gesture.

know_how.title: Cafés
know_how.text: Standing at the counter is usual and quick. Rounding up is a nice, optional thank-you.

know_how.title: Taxis
know_how.text: Round up to the next euro, a little more if the driver helps with bags.

know_how.title: Hotels
know_how.text: About €1 to €2 per bag for a porter. Lisbon and several Algarve towns add a nightly tourist tax at check-in, often not in the booking price.

know_how.title: Mondays
know_how.text: Many museums and monuments close on Mondays. Plan beaches, markets or Sintra's parks instead.

know_how.title: Shoes
know_how.text: Lisbon's hills and polished stone pavements get slippery, especially when wet. Flat shoes with grip make a big difference.

know_how.title: Bags
know_how.text: Keep bags zipped and in front on Tram 28, in crowds and at viewpoints. Pickpockets work the busiest spots.

know_how.title: Beaches
know_how.text: Check the lifeguard flag: red means no swimming. Outside the summer season, many beaches have no lifeguard. Atlantic water is cool even when the air is warm.

emergency_note: Pharmacies have a green cross sign. Each town keeps one pharmacy open late on a rota; the address is posted on every pharmacy door.

travel_notes: In Lisbon an espresso is a bica. Order it at the counter, like the locals.
The wave patterns underfoot are calçada portuguesa, small stones laid by hand, one by one.
Pastéis de nata are best warm, with a dusting of cinnamon and a little powdered sugar.
Many building fronts are covered in tiles, azulejos, which keep houses cool and shrug off the rain.
In the Algarve, cataplana is both a seafood stew and the clam-shaped copper pan it is cooked in.
Ginjinha, a sour cherry liqueur, is sold by the shot from tiny bars near Rossio.
